description: We’re the team behind EarthVision, a decision-support tool built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge’s Field Shift challenge. EarthVision combines NASA POWER climate data with local soil information, crop characteristics, and farmers’ priorities to compare three crop rotation strategies. Farmers can select their location on an interactive map, explore trade-offs in water demand, soil cover, and production potential, and download a report to help plan their next growing season.
summary: EarthVision is a web app that helps farmers and agronomists plan their next crop rotation using NASA Earth observation data. The user picks a field on the map, enters the current crop, soil texture, planting window and main priority (water, soil health or production). EarthVision then compares three rotation strategies against a full year of NASA POWER climate history for that location. It addresses the Field Shift challenge: rotation decisions are often made without local climate evidence, and EarthVision turns satellite-derived data into a clear, explainable comparison of benefits and risks, plus a PDF report.
details:
Problem. Crop rotation affects water use, soil health and income. Many producers, especially in Brazil’s grain belt, choose the next crop by habit or market alone, without checking how rainfall, temperature and solar radiation behave in their own region during the planting window. When the next crop doesn’t fit the local climate, the results are water stress, low yields, soil degradation, and pests and diseases that build up when the same plant family is repeated.

Solution. EarthVision is an exploratory decision-support tool that connects NASA climate data to a farmer’s own field profile. It recommends and ranks three rotation strategies:

  • Commercial grains: keeps grain production with a different species, e.g. soybean → corn.
  • Soil cover: grasses such as millet or sorghum, whose straw protects the soil.
  • Water efficiency: crops with lower water demand, such as sorghum or beans.

How it works.

  1. The user selects a sample location (Sorriso-MT, Rio Verde-GO, Londrina-PR or Barreiras-BA), clicks anywhere on the map, or enters coordinates.
  2. The browser queries the public NASA POWER Daily API directly. No credentials are needed. It requests the full 2025 calendar year for temperature, corrected precipitation and solar radiation (AG community).
  3. Daily values are aggregated into monthly series and annual indicators: mean temperature, total rainfall, mean radiation and number of dry months. The app shows how many valid days each value is based on.
  4. The user enters the current crop, soil texture, irrigation, a 4-month planting window and a priority.
    • Water: window rainfall compared with the crop’s indicative water demand, based on FAO and Embrapa references.
    • Soil: change of botanical family, ground cover, and soil texture.
    • Production: how well the window’s temperature fits the crop’s range, and the strategy’s purpose.
      The final score is weighted by the user’s priority.
  5. The app lists benefits and risks for each strategy (e.g. “repeats the botanical family”, “rainfall below indicative demand under rainfed conditions”) and exports a PDF report with the methodology, limitations and sources.

Key features.

  • Interactive map (Leaflet + OpenStreetMap) with point selection anywhere
  • Live NASA POWER data with monthly charts (Recharts)
  • Field profile saved in the browser
  • Three rotation strategies, ranked by priority-weighted scores
  • Transparent methodology and explicit limitations shown in the app
  • One-click PDF report (jsPDF)
  • Offline fallback: original NASA POWER response for Sorriso-MT bundled in the app
  • Automated tests (Vitest); built with React, TypeScript and Vite

Impact. EarthVision gives small and medium producers, extension agents and agronomy students free, transparent access to NASA climate evidence. It helps them avoid rotations that conflict with local rainfall and temperature, encourages family diversification and soil cover, and supports conversations between farmers and technical advisors. The scoring is intentionally explainable and is meant as a screening tool, not a replacement for agronomic advice. Next steps include multi-year climate normals, soil moisture (SMAP) and vegetation indices (MODIS/Landsat NDVI).
